name: Achilles Tendinopathy
summary: The Achilles tendon joins the calf muscles (gastrocnemius and soleus) to the heel bone (calcaneus). It handles very high loads in walking, running and jumping.

looksLike: Pain and stiffness in the tendon, worst in the morning and at the start of activity, often easing with warm-up and then returning after activity.
Tenderness and sometimes a firm, thickened area in the tendon.
Pain with running, jumping, hopping, stairs or calf raises.
Insertional type: pain at the back of the heel, worse with ankle dorsiflexion (for example going uphill or heel drops off a step) and tight shoes.
redFlags: Sudden pop, inability to rise on the toes, positive Thompson test, palpable gap
Pain after recent fluoroquinolone antibiotic or steroid use
Hot red swollen heel with fever
Bilateral heel pain with morning stiffness and other joint or skin signs
Thick painless bilateral nodules with a family history of heart disease
firstSteps: Initial approach: exclude rupture, then education, load management and progressive loading.
Justifying findings: localised tendon pain and thickening, reduced heel raise capacity, no rupture signs.
Priority: build tendon and calf capacity.

assess: Observe both Achilles tendons for swelling, nodules and heel position, and note footwear.
Palpate the tendon along its length (pinch it between finger and thumb), the insertion, the retrocalcaneal bursa and the area around the heel.
Ankle dorsiflexion and plantar flexion range.
Calf strength and endurance (single-leg heel raise, number of repetitions and quality).
Hop tests or hopping when tolerated.
Lumbar and neurological screen if indicated.

blocks.text: The **Achilles tendon** joins the calf muscles (gastrocnemius and soleus) to the heel bone (calcaneus). It handles very high loads in walking, running and jumping. **Achilles tendinopathy** is a load-related tendon problem with pain, sometimes swelling and reduced load tolerance. It is not a simple inflammation, and the older term tendinitis is no longer preferred [Ref - to verify].
Two main types are described:

rows: About 2 to 6 cm above the heel bone
Most common; often in runners and in active middle-aged people
Where the tendon attaches to the heel bone
May involve the bone, a bursa or a bony prominence; needs modified loading

blocks.text: Risk factors include a rapid rise in training, age, higher body weight, some medicines (fluoroquinolone antibiotics, corticosteroids) and some metabolic conditions [Ref - to verify]. Pain is real and often improves with a structured loading program, though recovery can take months.

blocks.text: E1. Palpation of the tendon

rows: Prone with the feet hanging off the bed
Palpate the tendon with a pinch grip from the heel up to the calf. Note thickening, a nodule and the most tender point
Localised tenderness and thickening that reproduces the familiar pain
Tenderness is also present in partial tears and paratendinopathy; interpret with other findings [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E2. Painful arc sign

rows: Help separate a tendon problem from tissue around the tendon
Find the thickened tender area and ask the patient to move the ankle up and down. Note whether the swelling moves with the tendon and whether pain stays in the same part of the arc
The swelling moves with the tendon, and pain appears in a part of the movement arc that changes with ankle position
Positive for tissue around the tendon (paratendinopathy)
Swelling stays still and pain is the same through the arc
Subjective; accuracy is limited [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E3. Royal London Hospital test

rows: Palpate the tender area with the ankle in dorsiflexion and then in plantar flexion. In tendinopathy the tenderness lessens or disappears when the tendon is held tight in plantar flexion (the tender area moves with the tendon)
Limited accuracy; used with the painful arc sign [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E4. Single-leg heel raise capacity

The patient stands on one leg and rises onto the toes as many times as possible with good height and control. Compare with the other leg. Reduced capacity or pain shows reduced load tolerance. Record the number as a baseline [Ref - to verify; avoid quoting norm values until sourced].
E5. Thompson (Simmonds) test for rupture

rows: Prone with the feet hanging off the bed, or kneeling on a chair
No foot plantar flexion on the affected side
The foot moves into plantar flexion
A positive result suggests Achilles rupture and needs urgent referral
A negative test does not rule out a partial tear. Also check for a palpable gap and weak heel raise

blocks.text: E6. Outcome measure

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Positive Thompson test or palpable gap? **Yes:** urgent referral.
Pain and thickening in the tendon 2 to 6 cm above the heel, load-related, with reduced heel raise capacity? **Yes:** working diagnosis is midportion Achilles tendinopathy.
Pain at the heel attachment with dorsiflexion provocation? **Yes:** working diagnosis is insertional Achilles tendinopathy.
Start a loading program with load management. Modify the program for insertional type.
If no improvement after a full trial, review the diagnosis and consider specialist options.

rows: Deep friction massage on the tendon

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education and progressive loading. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct. Do not claim to break down scar tissue or realign tendon fibres through manual techniques.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** progressive tendon loading is the first-line treatment. Both eccentric heel drops and heavy slow resistance programs have shown benefit, and no program is clearly superior for everyone [Ref - to verify]. Choose the one the patient can do and adhere to. Pain up to about 4 out of 10 during exercise is commonly accepted if it settles within 24 hours and morning stiffness is not worse the next day [Ref - to verify].

rows: Stand with the heels at floor level and rise to
5 holds of 30 to 45 seconds, once or twice a day [Ref
mid-range, hold; or seated with weight on the knee
Seated and standing calf raise (heavy slow resistance)
Rise slowly over about 3 seconds, lower over about 3 seconds, adding weight
3 sets of 15, then reduce to 12, 10, 8 repetitions as load goes up; 3 days a week for about 12 weeks [Ref - to verify]
Able to complete the sets with good control
Stand on a step with the knee straight (and again bent), rise on both feet, lower on the affected leg only
3 sets of 15, twice a day, daily for about 12 weeks [Ref - to verify]
Pain settles; add load with a backpack
Pain stays under about 4 out of 10 with no next-day flare

blocks.text: **Insertional type modification:** avoid dropping the heel below the level of the step (do the heel raise on flat ground or with the heel at step level) and avoid deep dorsiflexion stretches and tight shoes. Heel lifts in shoes may help comfort for a time [Ref - to verify].
**Load management:** reduce painful activity rather than stopping completely. Consider replacing some running with cycling or swimming. Keep a log of pain and morning stiffness.

**Return to running criteria (example):** no more than mild pain, good heel raise capacity compared with the other side, normal walking, and tolerance of hopping. Increase volume and intensity gradually.

rows: Option for persistent pain after several months of loading

blocks.text: **Medical options (decided by doctors):** corticosteroid injection into or near the tendon is generally avoided because of rupture risk. Other injections and surgery are for persistent cases after a long course of non-surgical care [Ref - to verify].

blocks.text: **Case:** A 38-year-old recreational runner has 3 months of Achilles pain 4 cm above the heel, worst in the morning. The tendon is thickened and tender. Single-leg heel raise reproduces his pain, with fewer repetitions than the other leg. Thompson test is negative. He recently started a new running plan with more hills.

**Working diagnosis:** midportion Achilles tendinopathy. **Plan:** education, reduce hills and speed, isometrics for pain, progressive slow heavy calf loading for 12 weeks, plyometrics later, gradual return to hills.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why is the Thompson test done? It helps detect a complete rupture, which needs urgent treatment, and which can be mistaken for tendinopathy or a calf strain.
Why are fluoroquinolone antibiotics and steroids asked about? They are associated with tendon damage and rupture [Ref - to verify].
Why is the insertional type loaded differently? Deep dorsiflexion compresses the tendon against the heel bone and can increase pain.
The patient wants complete rest. What do you say? Complete rest reduces load capacity and often does not cure the problem. Reduce, not remove, the load and build capacity.
Why measure the single-leg heel raise? It is a simple function test that shows reduced capacity and gives a baseline for progress.
**Initial approach:** exclude rupture, then education, load management and progressive loading.
**Justifying findings:** localised tendon pain and thickening, reduced heel raise capacity, no rupture signs.
**Priority:** build tendon and calf capacity.
**Manual therapy:** minor adjunct.
**Exercise:** isometrics, heavy slow or eccentric loading, then energy storage and sport drills.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** it is common and treatable; it takes months; keep moving within limits.
**Avoid:** complete rest, deep friction, steroid injection into the tendon, ignoring rupture signs.
**Measure:** VISA-A, heel raise, pain, stiffness.
**If no improvement:** specialist review.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** function restored and a maintenance calf strength plan.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult, no rupture, no systemic cause.

items: **Can be tested:** whether eccentric, heavy slow and isometric programs differ; whether shockwave adds benefit.
**Hypotheses:** that loading improves tendon capacity and pain through neural as well as structural changes.
**Future questions:** the best dose, and how to prevent recurrence.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.
